picked.t: Hundreds queue from dawn in overloaded Ho Chi Minh City cancer hospital
picked.body: At around 5 a.m. on Oct. 6, the second branch of Ho Chi Minh City Oncology Hospital in Thu Duc is already packed, with long lines of people waiting to get queue tokens to see the doctor. The hospital has chairs, but there were not enough for all the visitors. The facility receives 4,800 to 5,000 people every day, including about 700 for radiotherapy, with most coming from provinces and cities across the country. The hospital has 10 radiotherapy machines working in three shifts, from 5 a.m. to 11 p.m. every day. For the machines to deliver their first radiation treatment at 5 a.m., technical staff must arrive between 3 and 4 a.m. to perform checks, measurements, and quality assurance procedures. The radiotherapy department opens at 5 a.m., but half an hour earlier their seating areas and corridors are already crowded with patients waiting for treatment. According to Dr. Diep Bao Tuan, director of the Ho Chi Minh City Oncology Hospital, the 10 radiotherapy machines are running at full capacity and treating about 700 patients a day, but another 800-1,000 people remain on the waiting list. Patients wait an average of four to six weeks for their turn. According to Dr. Diep Bao Tuan, director of the Ho Chi Minh City Oncology Hospital, the 10 radiotherapy machines are running at full capacity and treating about 700 patients a day, but another 800-1,000 people remain on the waiting list. Patients wait an average of four to six weeks for their turn. Each patient waits for about an hour for their radiotherapy session. Many, exhausted, sleep on benches along the corridors. To cut the time needed to change equipment and accessories between sessions, the hospital often schedules patients with similar conditions consecutively. These are among the measures being used while the hospital waits for additional capacity. Bong, a 63-year-old woman from An Giang, came to Ho Chi Minh City for treatment for endometrial cancer. After surgery in June, she waited for a month and a half before beginning radiotherapy. She chose the first session of the day at 5 a.m. so that she could finish early and return to her rented room to rest. She is now on her 21st out of 28 sessions. For the treatment, she has paid an advance of VND10 million (US$385) after the amount covered by health insurance was deducted. A 59-year-old man from Gia Lai in the Central Highlands sat waiting in a corner of the department corridor from early morning. He had surgery for a meningioma a year earlier but did not undergo the recommended radiotherapy because he believed the tumor was benign. When the disease recurred, he had to undergo a second operation followed by radiotherapy. After surgery, he waited for more than two months to begin radiotherapy. "At first, the doctor said I would have to wait six weeks, but it ended up being eight," he said. " I was worried because the disease had already come back once, but with so many patients, there was nothing else I could do." Radiotherapy is not the only service under pressure; Other areas are also crowded from before dawn. The overload is expected to ease somewhat since Ho Chi Minh City recently approved more than VND5 trillion (US$192.5 million) to expand the hospital in 2026-2030. The expansion will include a new high-tech disease screening center, purchases of specialized medical equipment including a cyclotron system and single-energy linear accelerator, a new proton therapy center, and a new support facility for patients. The city is also developing a multi-tier healthcare network, including the Oncology Hospital's Ba Ria and Binh Duong campuses and medical clusters in Tan Kien and Thu Duc, in an effort to expand cancer treatment capacity and reduce pressure on existing facilities. picked.t: Casting nets: floodwaters bring seasonal bounty to Vietnam's Mekong Delta
picked.body: The annual flood season is a natural cycle in the Mekong Delta, typically lasting from August to November. As water from the Mekong River and upstream areas flows into the region, vast areas of farmland become submerged. While the flooding can disrupt daily life and agriculture, it also replenishes nutrients in the soil and creates favorable conditions for fish, shrimp and other aquatic species to thrive, providing local communities with an important seasonal source of food and income. The annual floods also help clean the fields, eliminate weeds and pests, and deposit nutrient-rich alluvial soil. In this photo taken in Dong Thap Province, residents take their fishing gear into the fields to catch local specialties such as cyprinid fish, shrimp, crabs and eels, as the floodwaters arrive. After more than 30 years of making a living by setting fishing traps, Le Van Son, from Thuong Lac Commune, Dong Thap, said his income depends on how high the water rises. Only when the water spreads across the fields and remains there for an extended period does it bring in large quantities of shrimp and fish. "This job is enough to get us through a few months of the flood season, but it does not leave us with much extra," he said. Flying minnow, a small fish familiar to Mekong Delta residents, appears in large numbers during the flood season. The fish grows to only about the size of a finger, has tender meat and is commonly braised with pepper, deep-fried or cooked in soup. During the flood season, it is relatively cheap, selling for VND10,000-15,000 (US$0.38-0.58) per kilogram fresh, while dead fish sold as bait for larger fish can cost just a few thousand dong. Brothers in An Hoa Commune, Dong Thap, head into the inundated field carrying nets to set fish traps. A flood level of roughly half a meter creates optimal working conditions, reducing the physical strain of wading through deep water while extending the window to harvest seasonal aquatic specialties. Flood-season catches provide the essential raw materials powering Hong Ngu Ward's traditional dried freshwater fish craft village in Dong Thap. Home to roughly 20 households engaged in the production, the village is renowned for its dried snakehead, gourami, and catfish. People clean, butterfly, salt, and season the fresh catch before laying the fish out to dry under the sun, a time-tested process that locks in their natural sweetness. Wet markets swell with an influx of freshwater crabs and fish during the flood season, with supplies driving prices lower than in the dry months. At Hong Ngu Market, crab vendor Duong Thi Huynh Nhu purchases hundreds of kilograms of crabs daily to keep up with brisk demand. Nhu sells large crab claws separately for VND280,000 to VND300,000 per kilogram, while the remaining meat is finely ground to prepare rieu , a traditional Vietnamese crab soup base. "The flood season is such a good time to sell," Nhu noted. picked.t: 9 Asian cities food lovers shouldn't miss in 2026, including Ho Chi Minh City
picked.body: The list highlights how local ingredients, generations of cooking traditions, and modern kitchens make each destination worth a food-focused trip. HCMC is Vietnam's only representative, joining Seoul, Taipei, Hong Kong, Manila, Singapore, Penang, Bangkok and Tokyo. Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam Street food is a major draw in HCMC, where bowls of pho and neighborhood coffee shops offer a taste of everyday life. Young chefs are giving familiar Vietnamese ingredients fresh expression, building seasonal menus that connect contemporary cooking with the flavors of everyday meals. Michelin highlighted CieL, a restaurant taking a modern approach to Vietnamese ingredients, and ST25 by KOTO, named after the Vietnamese rice variety that features in several of its dishes. Together, they illustrate the city's growing culinary range: visitors can explore local flavors at street level, then discover how chefs develop those same foundations in a restaurant setting. Seoul, South Korea Seoul rewards an appetite for specialties. Many of its most characteristic restaurants concentrate on a single dish, whether a clear, deeply flavored beef broth or raw crab steeped in marinade. Fermented pastes and sauces give much of the city's cooking its distinctive depth. Those flavors also underpin contemporary Korean dining. At Mingles, a three-Michelin-starred restaurant, traditional ingredients are woven into modern tasting menus. From a neighborhood soup house to an ambitious dining room, Seoul offers different ways to discover the care and complexity behind Korean cooking. Taipei, Taiwan Beef noodles, braised pork rice, and steamed buns filled with meat provide an inviting introduction to Taipei. These everyday favorites also help shape the city's contemporary restaurants, where the flavors of street stalls and night markets remain important reference points. Taipei's chefs bring a local accent to international cooking. At Eika, a contemporary Japanese restaurant, fermented tofu and soy milk find their way into carefully composed menus. For travelers, moving between night markets and restaurants reveals how Taiwanese ingredients and tastes give imported cuisines a character of their own. Hong Kong Roast goose, wonton noodles, char siu barbecued pork, and dim sum remain central to Hong Kong's food culture. Busy noodle shops and lively dining halls offer some of the most direct ways to experience it. The city's appeal also lies in its breadth. Restaurants serving the regional cuisines of Ningbo, Shanghai, and Shunde sit alongside an international dining scene. Amber, a three-Michelin-starred French restaurant known for dairy-free cooking, represents another direction. Visitors can explore both longstanding Chinese traditions and contemporary experimentation. Manila, Philippines In Manila, family recipes and regional traditions are giving chefs a rich foundation for contemporary cooking. Michelin highlighted slowly simmered broths, carefully judged sourness and familiar flavors, with technique supporting the food rather than dominating it. Linamnam, an intimate restaurant with just 10 covers, reflects that approach through dishes rooted in the chef's memories and local traditions. Beyond individual restaurants, shared plates and leisurely meals are part of the attraction. Exploring a neighborhood over several meals offers visitors a taste of both Filipino cooking and the social life surrounding it. Singapore Singapore's hawker stalls and fine-dining restaurants draw inspiration from one another. Michelin noted that techniques once associated with elaborate tasting menus are appearing in modest stalls, while restaurant chefs increasingly turn to familiar local flavors. Travelers can begin with noodles at a hawker center, a collection of food stalls, before exploring contemporary cooking at Seroja, a restaurant inspired by the culinary traditions of the Malay Archipelago. Across different budgets and settings, this exchange gives visitors a way to taste the city's multicultural identity. Penang, Malaysia Penang's food culture is rooted in dishes such as wok-fried flat rice noodles, tangy fish-based noodle soup, and rice served with an assortment of curries. These street-food staples reflect the island's mix of communities and remain central to everyday eating. Contemporary restaurants draw on that same heritage. In George Town, Penang's capital, restored buildings provide distinctive settings for new dining experiences. Au Jardin, a restaurant in a former bus depot, combines French technique with local flavors. Eating at both street stalls and modern restaurants reveals different expressions of the island's culinary traditions. Bangkok, Thailand Bangkok's chefs are looking more closely at Thailand's regional recipes and seasonal produce. Menus increasingly identify farmers and ingredient origins, giving diners a clearer sense of where their food comes from.
